title: World Court to rule on 19 November in Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar
dek: The International Court of Justice will give its final judgment in The Gambia's case, seven years after it was filed. About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees live in Bangladesh, most in camps near the Myanmar border.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) will deliver its judgment in the genocide case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar over the treatment of the Rohingya on Thursday, 19 November, at 10 am in The Hague (2:30 pm IST). The court announced the date in a press release on 3 November.

The ruling will decide whether Myanmar, as a state, broke the 1948 Genocide Convention during the military campaign that began in northern Rakhine State in August 2017. It is not a criminal trial of individuals. ICJ judgments are final and binding, and cannot be appealed.

## The case

The Gambia, a small West African country, filed the case in November 2019 with the backing of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. It says Myanmar's security forces carried out killings, rape and the burning of villages with the intent to destroy the Rohingya, a mostly Muslim minority, as a group. At least 730,000 Rohingya fled into Bangladesh during the 2017 operations, the Myanmar news outlet DVB reported.

Myanmar has denied genocide throughout. Its military describes the 2017 offensive as a counter-terrorism operation that followed coordinated attacks on border police posts by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, an armed group. Myanmar tried to have the case thrown out on preliminary objections, but the court confirmed in July 2022 that it had jurisdiction.

The court's 15 judges heard the arguments on the merits from 12 to 29 January 2026, including closed sessions where witnesses testified, according to Impunity Watch. Eleven countries have intervened in the case, the court's case title shows. To prove genocide, a court must find a specific intent to destroy a protected group, in whole or in part. That is a high bar: DVB notes that this will be only the third final judgment on the merits in a state genocide case in the court's 80-year history, after the cases involving Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia and Serbia.

## Why it matters for Bangladesh and India

Bangladesh carries most of the cost of the crisis. The UN refugee agency (UNHCR) counted 1,184,864 Rohingya refugees in Cox's Bazar district at the end of February 2026, up by nearly 179,000 in a year as fighting in Rakhine State pushed new arrivals across the border. In June, UNHCR warned that its 2026 response plan for Bangladesh, at $710.5 million, was 26% smaller than last year's and covered only the minimum needed to save lives.

The verdict will matter for any eventual return of refugees to Myanmar, which Dhaka has long sought. It also has a direct bearing on India's eastern neighbourhood. Rakhine State borders Bangladesh and lies on the route of India's Kaladan transport project, which links Kolkata's port with Mizoram through Myanmar. Instability there affects both the project and the border regions of Bangladesh, Mizoram and Manipur.

> The judgment "will mark a crucial moment in the Rohingya's quest for justice." — Maria Elena Vignoli, Human Rights Watch

DVB also notes that the ruling is likely to be read closely for its reasoning on genocidal intent, which is at issue in South Africa's separate case against Israel over Gaza. Israel denies the accusation in that case.

## What happens next

The president of the court, Judge Iwasawa Yuji, is expected to read the judgment at a public sitting. If the court finds against Myanmar, it can order the country to take measures, but it has no police force of its own: a state that believes a judgment is being ignored can take the matter to the UN Security Council, where China and Russia, both of which have close ties with Myanmar's military government, hold vetoes. Myanmar is already under provisional measures the court ordered in January 2020, requiring it to prevent genocidal acts and preserve evidence.
